title: MA8-08387
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, the claimant, 26 years old, a citizen of Mexico, is basing his refugee protection claim on sections 96-membership in the particular social group of homosexuals-and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). In support of his claim, he is alleging the following facts.
The claimant alleged that he is homosexual and that his problems with his lover began in XXXX 2008.
He had been in a romantic relationship with XXXX since XXX 2006.

In March 2008, he met a prominent politician, XXXX, at the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. XXXXX displayed an interest in the claimant by giving him expensive presents and asking him out several times. A month later, they became lovers and started having a secret affair because of XXXXX high social standing in the community.

The claimant ended this relationship with XXXXX because he was not proud of deceiving XXXXX. XXXX was offended and started harassing the claimant. One day, he told the claimant that he was going to get rid of XXXX because he could not let go of his relationship with the claimant.
At this time, the claimant began noticing strange people where he and XXXX lived.

Tired of the threats, the claimant warned XXXXX that if he did not leave him alone, he would reveal the cards, gifts and photographs that XXXXX had given him-undeniable evidence of the relationship that would damage XXXXX image in the community.

A few days later, the police called the claimant to tell him that XXXX had been killed. The claimant went to the police station to identify the body. The claimant wanted to report XXXXX threats to the police, but he changed his mind when they made fun of him after he told them that XXXX was his lover.

The claimant went to live with a friend. The next day, XXXXX called the claimant on his cellphone to warn him that he knew where he was. The claimant went to seek refuge in the city of XXXXX. However, two days later, XXXXX called him again. He said that it was his last chance to go back to him; if he refused, he would kill him that same day.

The claimant immediately his changed telephone number and travelled to XXXXXXXX. However, six days later, XXXXX called him on his cellphone again and warned him that he was going to kill him within 24 hours.
Fearing for his life, the claimant left his country on XXXXX, 2008.
He claimed refugee protection in Montréal on June 27, 2008.
After hearing the claimant's testimony and analyzing all of the evidence, the panel determines that this claim cannot be allowed, for the following reasons.

Based on the claimant's testimony, according to which he married XXXXX on XXXXXX, 2010, in Montréal, the panel concludes that there is a nexus with one of the five grounds in section 96, that is, membership in the particular social group of homosexuals. Identity

The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction. He appeared before the authorities at the port of entry with his Mexican passport, which was seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC), and copies of which are on file.1 Plausibility and credibility
The claimant's testimony was not credible. The following are some examples.
The claimant testified that he still fears XXXXX because he is convinced that this individual will kill him as soon as he returns to Mexico.

When asked about XXXXX profile, the claimant testified that he is a well-known politician in XXXXX. When asked what political party XXXXX belongs to, the claimant answered the "XXX"; when asked what this acronym stood for, the claimant stated that it stood for the XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXX and that XXXXX had XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX 2008.

Despite the extensive amount of evidence submitted as A-1, the panel could not find a party called the [translation] "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX." The documentary evidence indicates that the Party XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, abbreviated XXX, is the second-largest parliamentary group in Mexico's chamber of deputies.

In addition, there is no information on a politician named XXXXXXXXXX in the extensive evidence entered on the record. Furthermore, there is no evidence to corroborate the claimant's statements that XXXXX was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in 2008. Consequently, the panel is of the opinion, based on the fact that XXXXX is not mentioned in the documentary evidence submitted and on a balance of probabilities, that XXXXX is not currently part of the political scene in Mexico. This leads the panel to question the truthfulness of the claimant's entire story. The following analysis supports this conclusion.

Asked to provide more information on the alleged affair between the claimant and XXXXX, the claimant testified that his affair with this individual began on XXXXX, 2008, and that he ended the relationship by telephone on XXXXX, 2008. When asked whether XXXXX had ever been to his home, he answered that XXXXX sometimes accompanied him to his door.

Questioned further about the dates on which the events took place, the claimant testified that his next face-to-face meeting with XXXXX was on XXXXX, 2008, at the XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, where the claimant worked. He also testified that it was on this date that XXXXX had mentioned that he was going to get rid of XXXXX.

The claimant also testified that it was on XXXXX, 2008, that he had noticed strange people in a pickup truck outside his home. He added that these were XXXXX employees. When asked to explain how he knew that, the claimant added that these people were members of XXXXX security staff. Questioned further, he added that these six security officers usually accompanied them to the various locations where the claimant and XXXXX met. In light of this testimony, the claimant was asked to explain why, in paragraph 10 of his narrative,2 he stated that he had [translation] "started noticing strange people" where he lived. He tried to explain that he had meant to say [translation] "that it was strange that these people were in his neighbourhood." The panel is not satisfied with that explanation, for the following reasons.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant clearly alleged in his narrative that the people outside his house were strange people or strangers, not [translation] "that it was strange that these people were in his neighbourhood." The panel is of the opinion that the claimant tried to brush aside the inconsistency, which the panel found to be flagrant. It is reasonable to expect the claimant to specifically and clearly disclose that he had recognized XXXXX security officers in his neighbourhood, if that was the case. The panel concludes that the inconsistency between his testimony and the information in his narrative undermines his credibility.

When asked whether he had had any contact with XXXXX between XXXX and XX, 2008, the claimant initially testified that they had talked on the telephone on XXXX; he then amended his testimony and stated that there had not been any contact between these dates.

Given this testimony, the panel asked the claimant about the date on which he allegedly threatened to reveal the cards, gifts and photographs from XXXXX. He answered, [translation] "After XXXXX was killed." In light of this testimony, the claimant was asked to explain why, in paragraph 11 of his narrative, he stated he had threatened XXXXX before XXXXX murder. The claimant testified that he was stressed and nervous, that he had confused the events and that he had threatened XXXXX on XXXX. This explanation does not satisfy the panel, for the following reasons.

It is reasonable to expect the claimant to speak about his alleged experiences with consistency, integrity and accuracy, since, according to his testimony, these events are the reason he does not want to return to his country.

The claimant testified that he sought refuge with a friend on XXXXX. He added that on XXXXX, XXXXX called him on his cellphone to warn him to return and that this was when he decided to flee from XXXXX and go to a friend's home in XXXXX. The claimant stated that he stayed in XXXXX for two or three days, and that on XXXXX, 2008, XXXXX called and warned him that he knew where he was and ordered him to return to XXXXX. And although the claimant changed his telephone number, XXXXX managed to call him on XXXXX, while he was still in XXXXXXX, because he wanted the claimant to give him the photographs and gifts that he had given him within 24 hours or else he would kill him.

The claimant subsequently testified that he had told XXXXX that he had the photographs; however, he had already deleted the photographs from his camera. When asked why there is no mention of any photographs in paragraph 15 of his narrative, the claimant answered, [translation] "I do not know." This explanation does not satisfy the panel, for the following reasons.

Throughout both his narrative and his testimony, the claimant alleged that XXXXX adamantly wanted to resume his romantic relationship with him. In the claimant's written allegations, XXXXX killed XXXXX for this reason alone.

However, in paragraph 15 of his narrative, the claimant stated that XXXXX last threats were "he told me he was going to kill me in 24 hours". When asked about this new element of his story, the claimant suddenly stated that what XXXXXX wanted was the incriminating [translation] "photographs." The panel concludes that the claimant added a new element to his story to embellish his refugee protection claim. The claimant is not credible.

When asked how XXXXX was killed, the claimant answered, [translation] "by gunshot." When asked whether the murder had been reported in the Mexican newspapers, the claimant testified that one newspaper report had described his murder as an attempted theft. When asked to explain why he had not submitted the newspaper article into evidence, the claimant testified that XXXXX name was not mentioned in the article and that he had not kept the article in question.

To corroborate XXXXX murder, at the outset of the hearing, the claimant submitted a faxed copy of an email from "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX," dated XXXXX, 2011. The panel attaches little probative value to this document, for the following reasons.

First, subrule 28(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules states the following: All documents used at a proceeding must be in English or French or, if in another language, be provided with an English or French translation and a translator's declaration.
No translator's declaration was provided in accordance with the requirements of rule 28.

Second, when asked who this person named XXXXXX was, the claimant testified that he was a lawyer, [translation] "a friend of a friend." The document does not contain a header, an address or even a personalized signature page, which is a relatively common practice for law firms and which would have indicated to the panel that this was indeed a legal, probative and relevant document.

Finally, although the content mentions the [translation] "deceased boyfriend, XXXXX..." and [translation] "the deceased's estate in Family Court...," the panel is of the opinion that there is no evidence in this document establishing that XXXXX was murdered as the claimant described.

The claimant also submitted into evidence, at the outset of the hearing, another fax of a copy of an email from "XXXXXXXXXXXXXX," dated XXXXXX, 2011. When asked about this person's identity, the claimant testified that he was one of his friends in Mexico. The panel attaches little probative value to this document, for the following reasons.

Once again, no translator's declaration was provided in accordance with the requirements of rule 28. Second, the content of this document, produced only one week before the hearing, is highly subjective and does not come from an independent and reliable source. Based on the inconsistencies in this file, the panel concludes that this document was produced solely for the purpose of embellishing the refugee protection claim.

Finally, the claimant was asked whether he had travelled outside Mexico before he travelled to Canada in XXX 2008. He testified that he had not. Consequently, he was asked why his passport was issued to him on XXXXXX, 2008, five weeks before he left for Canada. The claimant testified that he had planned to travel with XXXXX to Cuba for a vacation at the end of July 2008. Based on the inconsistencies in this file and on a balance of probabilities, the panel concludes that the claimant was intending to travel to Canada on XXXXXX, 2008, and not to Cuba, as alleged; he invented his story of being persecuted by XXXXX for the purpose of submitting a refugee protection claim one month after he arrived in Canada. State protection

It should be assumed that the state is capable of protecting its citizens, except in situations of complete breakdown of the state apparatus.3 The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens reinforces the principle that international protection comes into play only if the claimant has no alternative.4
A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must satisfy the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, the evidence establishes that state protection is inadequate.5

In this case, the claimant testified that he had not filed a complaint with the Mexican authorities because it was not worth it, given XXXXX influence in Mexico. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant's assertion that XXXXX had too much influence in Mexico is insufficient not to try to make use of all possible courses of action to obtain protection or to find out whether his country's authorities were able or willing to protect him.

Even if the panel believed that XXXXX was an influential politician, the fact remains that his influence would have been limited to the state of XXXXXXXX, because he lived in XXXXX. It seems reasonable to believe that the claimant could have sought protection in XXXXXX, in the state of XXXXX, a city more than 1,700 kilometres from XXXXX.

The panel rejects the claimant's explanation, finding it insufficient to explain why the claimant concluded that the authorities would not act on his complaint before he left his country. In doing so, the claimant failed to exhaust all possible courses of action in his country before seeking international protection.

The claimant must demonstrate that he has taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek state protection, given the context of the country in general. The claimant must also demonstrate the steps taken and his interaction with the authorities.6

The claimant is a national of Mexico, a country that, according to the documentation,7 functions normally and is not in a situation of complete breakdown. Therefore, the claimant's country is presumed to be capable of protecting him, and this requires him to seek this protection before claiming refugee protection elsewhere, in this case, here in Canada. The documentary evidence8 shows that Mexico is making an effort to protect its citizens, by putting structures in place and adopting measures to enable citizens to file complaints. They can file a complaint by telephone, in person or online via the Internet. In this case, there is nothing in the written or oral evidence demonstrating that the claimant made a serious and sufficient effort to obtain state protection or that he exhausted all courses of action open to him.

Having concluded that the claimant did not make a serious and sufficient effort to obtain state protection and that the claimant did not exhaust all courses of action open to him in his country, the panel finds that the claimant was unable to discharge his burden of rebutting the presumption of protection that the state of Mexico would be able to offer him.

To rebut the presumption of state protection, the claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect (absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national).9 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and have probative value, but must also satisfy the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection is inadequate.10

Consequently, the panel concludes that the claimant did not provide "clear and convincing" evidence that the Mexican state cannot or will not protect him. Membership in the particular social group of homosexuals

In his narrative, the claimant stated that, because of his sexual orientation, he faced discrimination in his environment for years. At school, the teachers showed no sympathy, and his peers mistreated him. He alleged that he had to change schools three times and that his parents beat him and threw him out of the house when they discovered that he was homosexual. He also alleged that he was dismissed several times over the years and that it was very difficult for him to find a stable job.
Although the panel accepts that the claimant is homosexual, it finds that the allegations of discrimination against him were exaggerated to embellish his claim, for the following reasons.

On August 15, 2011, the claimant submitted amendments to his Personal Information Form (PIF) to point out that he had attended six schools over the years and that he had worked in seven different locations between XXXXX 2003 and XXX 2005. However, at question 6 of his PIF, the claimant mentioned that he has 12 years of education, after attending one elementary school, one secondary school and one college. The panel sees nothing extraordinary about his school career.

The information provided by the claimant at page 5 of the document Schedule 1, "Background Information," submitted as A-1, Immigration File, is the same information that he provided in his initial PIF. When asked why he had not provided the same personal information that he provided in the amendments when he submitted his refugee protection claim, the claimant answered that he had not paid attention. This explanation does not satisfy the panel, for the following reasons.

When the claimant provided the information requested in this form, he declared that the information he gave was complete, true and correct. The panel notes that it is unreasonable for the claimant to wait until the day before his hearing to amend information as basic as his education and his list of employers. The panel concludes that the amendments were made at the last minute to harmonize the allegations in his narrative with respect to his homosexuality.

Finally, in the same document, when asked, "Who are you afraid of if you were to return to your country?" the claimant answered "XXXXXXXXX" There is no mention of discrimination or of persecution based on his homosexuality. The claimant did not have a satisfactory reason when he was asked to explain why he did not mention his sexual orientation.
In any event, the panel concludes that the discrimination alleged by the claimant does not amount to persecution. Internal flight alternative (IFA)
Alternatively, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant has an internal flight alternative in Mexico.

At the hearing, the claimant was asked what he might fear if he returned and lived elsewhere in Mexico, such as in the city of La Paz, a Mexican city on the Gulf of California coast and the capital of Baja California Sur, or in Mexico City in the Federal District.
The claimant testified that XXXXX would be able to find him anywhere in Mexico.

Although the panel made sure to give him the opportunity to support his evidence, the claimant submitted no reason why it would be unreasonable, within the meaning of the case law,11 to go to one of these cities to seek refuge. He also submitted no real and concrete evidence establishing the existence of conditions making it possible that he could run the risk of being persecuted on a Convention ground or face a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment.

As stated by the Honourable Justice Lagacé in Ramirez: ... The burden of proof regarding an internal flight alternative rests on the claimant. Thus, the applicant had to establish either that it would be unreasonable for him to seek refuge in another part of the country or that there were, in fact, conditions preventing him from relocating elsewhere....12

In Palacios, Justice Shore recalled what the case law has held several times: It is settled law that in matters concerning internal flight alternatives the burden of proof is on the applicant.... Therefore, the refugee claimant must demonstrate that it would be unreasonable for him or her to seek refuge in a different part of the country.13

In Thirunavukkarasu,14 the Court of Appeal established that the onus is on the claimant to demonstrate why, on a balance of probabilities, he faces a serious risk of persecution in a part of the country where there might be an internal flight alternative.
The claimant is a 26-year-old man with 12 years of education and 5 years of labour market experience in Mexico, as XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.
The incidents (which the panel does not believe) allegedly occurred in 2008, and the panel does not believe that XXXXX still has any interest in the claimant, given the passage of time.

In this case, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not discharge his burden of proof, as set out in the case law,15 and concludes that he has an internal flight alternative. This is a fatal consideration that "...is in itself sufficient to dispose of the refugee claim," as stated by the Honourable Justice Shore in Palacios,16 above, under either section 96 or subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

For all of these reasons, I determine that the claimant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, cannot succeed. The claimant's fear has no objective basis, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA, because he can avail himself of state protection.

Consequently, his refugee protection claim is rejected.
